title: Below Market Value Purchases
summary: Silver Oak Capital's Below Market Value (BMV) Purchases page (a Bridging sub-page in the site nav) explains that a BMV purchase is one where the buyer pays less than open market value; a high-street bank lends against the lower purchase price while a specialist BMV/bridging lender can lend against the higher open market valuation. The page uses a worked example (house worth £200,000 bought for £150,000: 75% of price = £112,500 leaving a £37,500 deposit, whereas 75% of value = £150,000 covers the whole price). It names three buyer situations (family sale at a discount, sitting tenant buying their rented home, professional investor buying from a distressed seller), says bridging lenders do not apply the six-month refinance restriction that mainstream mortgage lenders do, and stresses that the reason for the discount (the 'story') matters to lenders. H1, meta description, rates, fees, loan sizes, durations, process and CTAs were not revealed by the search results.

sections.heading: What is a below market value (BMV) purchase
sections.content: [a] A BMV purchase is a deal where the buyer pays less than the open market value of the property. The page is described as 'a specialist lending service for buying property below its open market value'.

sections.heading: How lenders treat BMV purchases: high street vs specialist
sections.content: [a] A high-street bank typically lends against the lower purchase price, while a specialist BMV lender can lend against the higher valuation. [b] A specialist BMV lender can often lend against the open market value rather than the discounted price. [b] Search summary across Silver Oak pages: 'offering lending on open market value, with bridging funds arranged in days'.

sections.heading: Worked example (£200,000 value / £150,000 price)
sections.content: [a] A £200,000 house bought for £150,000. A 75% loan on the purchase price gives a £112,500 mortgage, which leaves a £37,500 deposit to find. A 75% loan on the £200,000 value covers the whole £150,000 price. [b] 'A specialist BMV lender can often lend based on the £200,000 open market value.'

sections.heading: Who uses BMV finance
sections.content: [a] Three target buyer situations are named: family sales at a discount, sitting tenants buying the home they rent, and professional investors buying from distressed sellers.

sections.heading: Six-month refinance restriction
sections.content: [b] Bridging lenders don't apply the six-month refinance restriction that mainstream mortgage lenders do.

sections.heading: The 'story' behind the discount
sections.content: [b] The page stresses that the reason for the discount, or 'story', matters to lenders.

sections.heading: Legality (from sibling /faq/ page, surfaced in [b])
sections.content: [b] The FAQ page says the practice is legal, but misrepresenting the price to a lender is mortgage fraud: 'Buying a house for any agreed price is legal, but misleading a lender about the price is mortgage fraud.'
